1.pericope_label: Sing unto the Lord a new song: let them praise his name in the dance

schools.summary: Augustine makes the new song the difference between two men, the old man having an old song and the new man a new one, holds that whoever loves earthly things sings an old song however new his words, makes the new song one of peace and charity so that whoever severs himself from the union of the saints has followed old strife, and says his ears are not so much bent to hear the voice of the singer as to seek the deeds of the doer.

Gill allows the dance as an ancient practice but rather prefers the rendering with the pipe, and notices that the word for Maker in the second verse is plural; Calvin places the psalm at the return from captivity and reads it as encouragement to expect a full deliverance of which the permission to return was only a prelude, and keeps the new song comparative, the mark of some rare and unusual benefit.

Henry makes the song new by occasion and by affection, newly composed for each occasion and sung with new affections that keep old words from growing threadbare, keeps the dance and turns it against instrumental music, since those who urge music from this verse must by the same rule introduce dancing, and notices the plural in the word for Maker; Spurgeon makes the new song a duty of invention and observes that men are fonder of making new complaints than new psalms.

Clarke calls the psalm a song of triumph probably from the time of the Maccabees, notes that it has no title and no author’s name in the Hebrew or any version, takes the new song to mean the most excellent song and supports it from Latin usage with a line of a Latin poet before rounding on that poet’s English translator for a tame and inexpressive version, and denies that the word rendered dance ever means dancing anywhere in the Bible, holding that it always signifies a pipe.

Keil and Delitzsch report the patristic reading of the psalm as prophecy of the Maccabean wars and answer that it is explicable from the national self-consciousness of the period after Cyrus, place it in the restoration and assign it to the same hand as the preceding psalm, and warn that the New Testament church cannot pray as this psalm prays and that it has been the watchword of the most horrible errors; Ellicott dates it in the Maccabean age from the technical use of the word for the congregation, and gives four arguments for rendering the dance as a pipe.

debates: When was the psalm written? Keil and Delitzsch report that the fathers took it as prophecy of the wars of the Maccabees and answer that it is sufficiently explicable from the strengthened national feeling of the period after Cyrus, placing it in the restoration and comparing its standpoint with the book of Esther; Clarke keeps the Maccabean date as probable; Ellicott argues the same date from the technical use of the word for the congregation as a party name; Calvin puts it at the return from captivity and makes it an encouragement to expect the deliverance still to come.

Is the word in the third verse a dance or a pipe? Clarke denies that it or its cognate ever means dancing anywhere in the Bible and derives it from a root meaning to make a hole; Ellicott gives four arguments for the pipe, from the orchestral list in the next psalm, from a possible derivation, from an eastern version that renders it by the name of a flute still in use there, and from its pairing with the drum; Gill allows the dance but rather prefers the pipe; Henry keeps the dance and uses it as an argument against instrumental music in worship, since whoever urges music from the verse must by the same rule introduce dancing.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch warn against the psalm itself, holding that the New Testament church cannot pray as the Old Testament national church here prays, and that under the illusion that it might be used as a prayer without spiritual transmutation it has become the watchword of the most horrible errors; the block breaks off in the middle of the name of the man they cite for it.

Clarke turns from expounding the new song to attacking a famous English translation of the Latin line he has quoted for it, calling the version tame and inexpressive and exclaiming at the falling off.

Augustine holds that whoever does not sing with the whole earth sings an old song whatever words come out of his mouth, and that his own ears are not so much bent to hear the voice of the singer as to seek the deeds of the doer.
Gill and Henry both notice that the word for Maker in the second verse stands in the plural, Henry adding that some find the mystery of the Trinity in it.
themes: a psalm its own commentators warn about
new meaning excellent rather than recent
a dance translated out of the text
old words kept from growing threadbare
a plural noticed in the word for Maker

4.pericope_label: For the Lord taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation

schools.summary: Gill keeps the fourth verse to the pleasure God takes in his people, in their persons as accepted in Christ, in their services offered in faith and in their prosperity, and takes the glory of the fifth verse of the righteousness of Christ upon them now and the glory expected hereafter, while reporting a variant that reads in his glory and allowing a third sense in which the word is simply adverbial.

Clarke renders the beautifying as a making fair of the lowly and reports a Latin father who read it as an exalting of the meek in Jesus, holding that there is no other way for a humble soul to be exalted, reads the singing on beds as done reclining at a festal banquet, and adds that at the public entertainments of his own day a Latin line from another psalm is often sung to the same purpose, so that feasting is mingled with divine songs; Wesley makes the beautifying a matter of reputation before a world that now despises them.

Ellicott renders the line as an adorning of the oppressed with salvation and makes the figure literal, the honour won in the sight of the world being like a beautiful robe suggested by the actual triumphal dresses of the victors or by the spoils in which they appeared after the battle, and offers both readings of the couches without deciding, either a rejoicing carried far into the night or the divans on which feasts were held.

debates: What is the beautifying of the meek? Clarke makes it a making fair of the lowly and reports a Latin father who rendered it an exalting of the meek in Jesus; Ellicott makes it literal and military, an adorning with the triumphal dress or the spoils of the victors; Wesley makes it reputation before a world that now despises them; Gill keeps to the divine pleasure that lies behind it.

Are the beds beds or banqueting couches? Clarke reads the singing as done reclining at a festal banquet and notes that eating on couches is still practised in eastern countries; Ellicott allows either a rejoicing carried far into the night, so that the people burst out anew into singing after retiring to rest, or the divans on which feasts were held.
outliers: Clarke reports that at the public entertainments of his own day a Latin line from another psalm, giving the glory not to the singers but to God’s name for his mercy and truth, is often sung in imitation of this verse, so that feasting is mingled with divine songs.
Ellicott derives the figure of adorning from the actual triumphal dresses of the victors, or from the spoils in which they appeared after the battle.
Gill reports that some copies of one ancient version read not in glory but in his glory, which would make the object the glory of Christ seen now in the glass of the Gospel.
Gill and Clarke both allow that the word may be adverbial, so that the saints are to be gloriously joyful rather than joyful in a glory given them.
themes: a robe made out of captured spoil
beds that may be dining couches
a Latin grace sung at English dinners
glory given, glory seen, or glory as a manner
meekness beautified in the eyes of its despisers

6.pericope_label: Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand

schools.summary: Henry reads the verse as a job description, since those who taught Israel the high praises of the Lord also put a two-edged sword into their hand, and instances the leader of the exodus, the captain who took the land, and the king who was at once the sweet singer of Israel and the captain of its hosts, teaching their hands to war as God had taught his.

Gill spiritualises the whole armoury, the vengeance on the heathen becoming the apostles going out with the two-edged sword of the word so that the oracles were struck dumb and the temples forsaken, then vengeance on Rome in the latter days, and the kings bound with chains becoming emperors brought to the churches in chains of efficacious grace and made instruments in destroying persecuting princes; he also renders the mouth as the throat.

Clarke defuses the militancy four ways, setting the passage among the builders of the wall where every man wrought with one hand and held a weapon with the other, making the punishments fall on the treacherous of their own nation rather than on foreigners, keeping the binding of kings conditional on an attack that did not come, and allowing the later victories only as hyperbole not unusual in songs of triumph; at the last verse he asks outright whether the psalm promises the Church the dominion of the nations and answers that God never intended his Church to have the civil government of the world; Wesley keeps the vengeance literal and historical.

Ellicott renders the high praises as exaltations of celebration and corrects the mouth to the throat, offers three senses of the judgment written without choosing, a special order whose contents we could guess if we knew the occasion, the judgments registered in the sacred books and legitimate by prescription, or a still more general sense, and proposes a repunctuation by which the declaration about the honour of the saints stands as a separate written sentence; Keil and Delitzsch had already warned at the opening that the New Testament church cannot pray as this psalm prays.

debates: Does the psalm promise the Church dominion over the nations? Clarke puts the question in his own words at the last verse and answers that he does not think so, believing that God never intended his Church to have the civil government of the world and that the Church, like its Founder, will never be a ruler and divider among men; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same position from the other end of the psalm, holding that the New Testament church cannot pray as the Old Testament national church here prays; Gill, by contrast, keeps the conquest and transfers it to the sword of the word and the fall of Rome.

What is the judgment written? Ellicott offers three possibilities without choosing, a special order whose contents could be guessed if the occasion were known, the judgments registered here and there in the sacred books and so legitimate by prescription, or a more general sense of a recompense written before God; he then proposes a repunctuation by which the honour of the saints becomes a separate written declaration rather than part of the sentence executed.
outliers: Clarke keeps the binding of kings in the conditional mood, holding that if those kings and governors had attacked, God would have enabled his people to defeat them, and allows the later victories over the neighbouring nations only as hyperbole not unusual in poetry and in songs of triumph.

Clarke makes the punishments upon the people fall on the unfaithful and treacherous of their own nation, some of whose nobles had joined the enemies of the building and made alliances contrary to the law.

Clarke ends the psalm on a grim history, that Israel had this honour while it continued faithful, and that when it relapsed the city was taken and the temple burnt, more than a million slaughtered and the rest led captive and scattered.
Clarke observes that the Hebrew for a two-edged sword is literally mouth mouths.
themes: a psalm refused as a charter for rule
a sword held in the hand that builds
a written judgment nobody can identify
high praises moved from mouth to throat
